Q: Run a mysql command from a bat file without prompting for a password A:

Remove the quots you are using

[client]
user=user
password=xxxxx

that should solve it

Another solution can be running this once

mysql_config_editor set --login-path=local --user=user --password

Then in your bat file: you can use

mysql --login-path=local -e "YOUR SQL HERE"

even safer because credentials are encrypted

Also for client section to work MySQL should actually read the file sometimes the windows patterns are like this

  1. C:\ProgramData\MySQL\MySQL Server 8.0\my.ini

  2. C:\Program Files\MySQL\MySQL Server 8.0\my.ini

  3. Sometimes it doesnt read the MySQL file so you can use

    mysql --print-defaults

    This indicates which defaults are loading

Q: Codeigniter: Column 'id' in order clause is ambiguous A:

Generally, there are two ways to resolve the column ambiguity in a join query where two tables contain one or more identically named columns.

  1. As explained in 1052: Column 'id' in field list is ambiguous, you can "qualify" the source table of the column so that the database knows exactly which column you are referring to.

    return $this->db
    ->join('atommeta m', 'm.atom_id = a.atom_id')
    ->order_by('a.id')
    ->get('atoms a', $limit, $offset)
    ->result();
/*
SELECT *
FROM `atoms` `a`
JOIN `atommeta` `m` ON `m.atom_id` = `a.atom_id`
ORDER BY `a`.`id`
LIMIT 0, 10
*/

  2. For cases where the ambiguity specifically refers to identically named columns which are responsible for relating the tables, you can enjoy a USING() expression to disambiguate (and effectively consolidate those columns into a single reference).

    Specific to CodeIgniter, just use the shared column name as the second parameter of the join() call.

    I'll change the column in the ORDER BY clause to demonstrate the feature.

    return $this->db
    ->join('atommeta m', 'atom_id')
    ->order_by('atom_id')   // see, no table qualification
    ->get('atoms a', $limit, $offset)
    ->result();
/*
SELECT *
FROM `atoms` `a`
JOIN `atommeta` `m` USING(`atom_id`)
ORDER BY `atom_id`
LIMIT 0, 10
*/

Here are a few examples in a SQLize Demo.

The ambiguity error can occur in any clauses where a column can be referenced. The ambiguity error is a separate concern versus having two columns in the SELECT clause - where the last mentioned columns overwrite earlier-mentioned identically-named columns. For those issues, often "SELECT *" is to blame and the solution is explicit column referencing and aliasing.

Q: Difference between ArrayList and LinkedList in Java A:

Short answer: ALWAYS use ArrayList. In 99.9% of use cases. Because in 99% of the time, you just accumulate data. Maybe sort it. Then ArrayList is considerably better than LinkedList.

(When sorting large data comes into play, TreeMap and TreeSet or heap implementations are better)

The only time you SHOULD use something like a LinkedList/Queue/DeQue is when you have throughput, meaning: Adding at the end, taking at the front. And that is usually the case in multi-threaded environments. In which case you would use a LinkedBlockinQueue. So not even then a LinkedList itself.

So, apart from the obvious differences, like runtime complexity for accessing/removal etc, you should also consider things like cache-locality, additional RAM usage etc. Giving an ArrayList a proper initial size even nullifies its greatest weakness: Re-sizing of arrays for growing.

The ONLY reason I could think of is where you would use an actual LinkedList is

  • WHEN you explore structures like trees/graphs (file/directory tree, where you can find any amount of elements),
  • AND it's single-threaded,
  • AND you have to use something like a ToDo-List (like: Directory detected, but will handle it later),
  • AND you have to keep up the order (FIFO, for some strange reason; Normally one uses a Stack/ArrayList, which then reverses the order of processing: LIFO),
  • AND you do NOT use recursion on methods (which would negate the need for such a ToDo-List)
  • AND you do NOT care about duplicates (regarding file systems: the occurrence of links / symbolic links that maybe point to a resource already scanned or already in the ToDo-List)

So all in all, this is a pretty unlikely scenario.

Another point is the java.util.stream.Stream (filter, map, collect) paradigm, which replaces usage of most other Collections in Java anyways: Then you don't have to decide on the use of neither ArrayList NOR LinkedList.

Q: how do I use @importFrom so that it applies to a whole R package? A:

Although this is not a new question, it has been viewed thousands of time therefore, I guess, it should be answered.

It is not that easy to do it like that. The best way to proceed is to use the function use_import_from provided by the usethis package (included in the devtools package): usethis::use_import_from(package = "dplyr", fun = "bind_rows").

This will create/append a file named mypackage-package.R where mypackage is the name of your package. Its content looks like that:

#' @keywords internal
"_PACKAGE"

## usethis namespace: start
#' @importFrom data.table :=
#' @importFrom dplyr across
#' @importFrom dplyr group_by
#' @importFrom dplyr mutate
#' @importFrom dplyr n
#' @importFrom dplyr summarise
#' @importFrom magrittr %<>%
#' @importFrom magrittr %>%
#' @importFrom stats stepfun
## usethis namespace: end
NULL

And when you load/build the package, your namespace will be updated with something like:

importFrom(data.table,":=")
importFrom(dplyr,across)
importFrom(dplyr,group_by)
importFrom(dplyr,mutate)
importFrom(dplyr,n)
importFrom(dplyr,summarise)
importFrom(magrittr,"%<>%")
importFrom(magrittr,"%>%")
importFrom(stats,stepfun)

I hope that can help you.
